Technically yes it is possible. Printers are decently simple devices, just a few stepper motors and linear actuators. The ease of the mod would depend heavily on where the devices are comprised though. If it's on the driver level then a simple software patch on the computer would be possible. If it's on the hardware level it depends on whether or not the chips are rewritable. If they are then a software patch for the printer would need to be written, but the computer drivers would be usable. If it's in epprom then the host board would essentially have to be replaced, the easier option, or a device similar to a video game mod chip installed. The idea behind the mod chip is that it would sniff for the signal to write the dots and just not pass them to the rest of the hardware. Rebuilding a printer nowadays would actually be fairly easy thanks to the reprap project. Boards capable of running pretty much all the required hardware already exist. A translation layer between generic printer drivers and the new host board would have to be written, but that's not all that difficult of a task thanks to we'll laid out documentation from the Linux drivers team.

These dots are not added at the driver level. They are Introduced by the hardware, and on the models I am familiar with they are present even on internally generated test prints from the machine.

Most chips that control hardware in a modern copier/printer are ASIC's produced by the manufacturer and are not reprogrammable. You can reprogram certain portions of a machine's firmware/software through service modes if that data resides on flash ROM's or other storage media but I haven't seen an old style EPROM in a copier for many years.

Modern machines have data like this (serial numbers, meter counts, etc.) Stored in multiple locations on multiple circuit boards. For many, there is also a complicated series of "handshakes" between these boards to verify the integrity of that data.

I honestly can't think of a way, short of building your own device that would get rid of these dots. I believe that they are being introduced to the data stream after it is in raster and on it's way to be written by the laser. You, however might be able to introduce a random pattern of dots that would make it impossible to decode the non random pattern that the printer is producing.

I'll leave that work to someone else as it might cost me my job ;)
